United States, United Kingdom or the third one? The hospital that had rehearsed heart transplants for years did not do the first one. A team of thirty did it overnight on a grocer, and the patient woke up and spoke. He lived eighteen days; the next patient lived nineteen months; today half of recipients pass twelve years.
Guess before the map lights up, then see the hospital pinned and the survival numbers side by side.

research.topic: First human-to-human heart transplant: 3 December 1967, Groote Schuur Hospital, Cape Town, by Christiaan Barnard and a team of about 30; patient Louis Washkansky, 53, a grocer, lived 18 days (died of pneumonia). Donor Denise Darvall, 25, fatally injured by a car; her father Edward consented that night. Norman Shumway's Stanford team had developed the technique in dogs through the 1960s and performed the first US transplant on 6 January 1968. Second Cape Town patient Philip Blaiberg lived 19 months (593 days). ISHLT registry: median survival after adult heart transplant about 12–13 years.

myths.myth: The first heart transplant was American — Stanford invented the operation.
myths.reality: Shumway's Stanford team developed the technique, but the first human transplant was Barnard's in Cape Town on 3 December 1967; Stanford's first followed on 6 January 1968.

landscape.our_gap: Barnard clips are biographies or archive news; nobody erases the American assumption over the map, pins the hospital and stacks the 18-day / 19-month / 12-year survival silhouettes as a quiz.
